Kremsmunster
KREMS-mun-ster
n. (the Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 777, keeping the Tassilo Chalice and an eighteenth-century observatory tower)
German Kremsmunster, the minster on the Krems, from Munster, a monastery church.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kremsmunster in Upper Austria was founded in 777 by Tassilo III, duke of Bavaria, by tradition in memory of his son Gunther, killed by a boar while hunting in the valley. It keeps the Tassilo Chalice, a gilt copper cup of about 780 that is among the most important surviving objects of the Carolingian age, and the Codex Millenarius, an eighth-century gospel book. Between 1749 and 1758 the abbey built the Mathematical Tower, eight storeys of cabinets of natural history, physics and astronomy with an observatory on top, one of the earliest such towers in Europe. The dictionary records Kremsmunster for that tower, because it is a monastery taking the created order seriously, and for the order of knowing that Scripture insists on. Study begins with a disposition and not with an instrument, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10), and the understanding it yields is tested in obedience, “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments” (Psa 111:10). The failure mode of a learned institution is the one Nebuchadnezzar demonstrates on his own roof, “that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power” (Dan 4:30), and God states beforehand that He will not share the credit, “my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an observatory as a place for observing the heavenly bodies; a chalice as a cup or bowl; astronomy as the science of the heavenly bodies; a cabinet in this sense as a collection of curiosities; and a minster as a monastery, also a cathedral church.

expand to see more

OBSERVATORY, n. A place or building for making observations on the heavenly bodies.

CHALICE, n. A cup or bowl; usually, a communion cup.

ASTRONOMY, n. The science which teaches the knowledge of the celestial bodies, their magnitudes, motions and distances.

CABINET, n. A set of boxes or drawers for curiosities; also, a private room in which consultations are held.

MINSTER, n. A monastery; an ecclesiastical convent or fraternity; also, a cathedral church.

Key Scripture

Pro 9:10 — "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding."

Psa 111:10 — "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever."

Dan 4:30 — "The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?"

Isa 42:8 — "I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images."

Modern Corruption

Upper Austrian Benedictine abbey of 777 holding the Tassilo Chalice and an eight-storey observatory tower of 1749.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that natural philosophy has a proper home in a Christian house and a proper starting point. Kremsmunster stacked eight storeys of cabinets under an observatory, and the order of knowing is settled before the first instrument is bought, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).

The live temptation is the inversion, where learning becomes the ground of reverence instead of its fruit, and then the credit quietly changes hands. Scripture tests understanding by obedience, “his praise endureth for ever” (Psa 111:10); it records the exact words of a man surveying his own achievement, “Is not this great Babylon” (Dan 4:30); and it reports God's refusal to divide the honour, “I am the LORD: that is my name” (Isa 42:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yirah (H3374), fear, reverence; Hebrew sekel (H7922), prudence; Hebrew bana (H1129), to build; Hebrew kabod (H3519), glory.

expand to see more

Hebrew yirah (H3374) — fear, reverence, awe; “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”, Proverbs 9:10.

Hebrew daath (H1847) — knowledge, perception; “and the knowledge of the holy is understanding”, Proverbs 9:10.

Hebrew sekel (H7922) — prudence, discretion, good sense; “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments”, Psalm 111:10.

Hebrew bana (H1129) — to build, to establish; “that I have built for the house of the kingdom”, Daniel 4:30.

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; “my glory will I not give to another”, Isaiah 42:8.

Usage

"“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) — the order of knowing, settled first."

"“by the might of my power” (Dan 4:30) — the words of a man on his own roof."

"“my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8) — the credit God will not divide."
